title: The @Override Annotation
summary: Discover why the @Override annotation is an indispensable engineering safety net in Java: catching typo bugs, signature mismatches, and maintenance regressions at compile time.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and compilation semantics of the @Override annotation
Identify silent typo bugs that occur when omitting @Override
Learn how @Override protects codebases when superclass method signatures are refactored
Recognize that @Override is a compiler directive with SOURCE retention
expectedOutcomes: Ability to always write @Override on overridden methods for bulletproof compiler verification
Confidence explaining the difference between an accidental overload and an intended override

activities.title: The Legal Contract Signature Validator
activities.content:
Imagine you are signing an amendment to an existing corporate contract. You must adhere to the exact terms of Clause 4.2.

Without an automated validator, if you accidentally mistype the title as 'Clause 4.20', the legal department might accept the document as a brand-new, unrelated clause instead of modifying the existing one! The old Clause 4.2 remains active without you knowing, causing catastrophic legal disputes later.

The `@Override` annotation is an automated legal compliance validator: it explicitly tells the Java compiler: *'I intend to modify an existing parent method. If this method does not exactly match a method in my superclass, immediately halt and reject the code with an error!'*

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the @Override annotation in Java?
options: To tell the JVM to run the method on a separate background thread
To instruct the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a superclass or interface method
To make private methods accessible to subclasses
To force the method to be static
questions.explanation: @Override directs the compiler to check that the method matches an existing superclass or interface signature.

questions.question: Is the @Override annotation strictly required for method overriding to work in Java?
options: Yes, without @Override the compiler ignores the method
No, method overriding works without it, but @Override is strongly recommended to catch silent bugs
Only required in Java 8 and earlier
Only required for abstract methods
questions.explanation: Overriding works without @Override, but omitting it risks silent bugs from typos or accidental overloading.

questions.question: What happens if you annotate a method with @Override and mistype its name (e.g. 'toSting()' instead of 'toString()')?
options: The program compiles with a warning and creates an alias
A compile-time error occurs immediately
The JVM fixes the spelling error at runtime
The method is ignored
questions.explanation: The compiler immediately flags an error because no method named toSting() exists in any superclass.

questions.question: What happens if you place @Override on a method whose parameter list does not match the superclass method?
options: The method automatically overloads the parent method
A compile-time error occurs: Method does not override or implement a method from a supertype
The parameters are coerced into matching types
The superclass method is deleted
questions.explanation: @Override forces signature verification; any parameter mismatch causes compilation failure.

questions.question: What is the retention policy of the @Override annotation?
options: RUNTIME (preserved in bytecode and inspectable via reflection)
SOURCE (discarded by the compiler; does not exist in the .class file)
CLASS (retained in .class file but not loaded into JVM)
SYSTEM
questions.explanation: @Override has SOURCE retention; it exists solely for compiler verification and adds zero runtime overhead.

questions.question: Can you use the @Override annotation when implementing an interface method in Java 6 and later?
options: No, @Override can only be used on class inheritance
Yes, since Java 6, @Override is fully supported and recommended on interface method implementations
Only for functional interfaces
Only for default methods
questions.explanation: Java 6 expanded @Override to apply to interface method implementations as well as class overrides.

questions.question: What happens if a parent class method is renamed during refactoring, but subclasses have @Override on their implementations?
options: The subclasses silently break at runtime
The compiler immediately flags errors on all subclass methods, alerting engineers to update them
The JVM continues running the old method name
The refactoring tool deletes the subclasses
questions.explanation: @Override serves as an instant refactoring alarm, catching orphaned methods at compile time.

questions.question: Can @Override be applied to a static method?
options: Yes, if the static method has identical parameters
No, static methods cannot be overridden in Java, so applying @Override produces a compile error
Only in utility classes
Only if the method is public
questions.explanation: Static methods are hidden, not overridden. Applying @Override to a static method fails compilation.

questions.question: Can @Override be applied to a constructor?
options: Yes, to override the parent constructor
No, constructors cannot be overridden and cannot have @Override
Only default constructors
Only private constructors
questions.explanation: Constructors are never inherited or overridden, so @Override cannot be used on constructors.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most compelling reason to use @Override on every overridden method?
options: It makes the program run 50% faster
It prevents subtle, silent runtime bugs by turning accidental overloads into immediate compile errors
It is required by the JVM bytecode verifier
It allows methods to be called without an object
questions.explanation: The safety net of catching typos and signature mismatches at compile time is the primary benefit.

interviewQA.question: What is the purpose of the @Override annotation and why should you always use it?
interviewQA.answer: The @Override annotation is a compiler directive instructing the Java compiler to verify that the annotated method correctly overrides a method in a superclass or interface. It should always be used because it prevents catastrophic silent bugs caused by misspelled method names or accidental parameter mismatches, converting potential runtime disasters into immediate compile-time errors.

interviewQA.question: What happens under the hood with @Override during compilation and runtime?
interviewQA.answer: The @Override annotation has a retention policy of RetentionPolicy.SOURCE. During compilation, the Java compiler verifies that the method matches a supertype signature. Once compilation succeeds, the annotation is discarded; it is not stored in the .class bytecode file and incurs zero memory or runtime performance cost.

interviewQA.question: Can @Override be placed on static or private methods? Why?
interviewQA.answer: No. In Java, static methods are hidden rather than overridden, and private methods are not visible outside their declaring class. Attempting to place @Override on a static or private method results in a compilation error: 'The method must override or implement a supertype method'.

interviewQA.question: Can @Override be used when implementing methods from an interface?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. While Java 5 originally restricted @Override to class-to-class overrides, Java 6 expanded the annotation to cover interface implementations as well. In modern Java, it is best practice to annotate both class overrides and interface implementations with @Override.

interviewQA.question: How does @Override assist during large-scale enterprise refactoring?
interviewQA.answer: In large enterprise microservices or monolithic libraries, modifying a base class method signature can silently break dozens of downstream subclasses if they don't use @Override (they turn into unused overloads). With @Override, the compiler immediately flags every impacted subclass, allowing developers to refactor with complete confidence.

interviewQA.question: Give an example of a common bug caused by omitting @Override.
interviewQA.answer: A classic example is overriding equals(). The Object class declares 'public boolean equals(Object obj)'. If a developer writes 'public boolean equals(Employee e)' without @Override, this is an overload, not an override. Collections like HashSet and ArrayList still call equals(Object), resulting in broken duplicate detection and elusive bugs.

activities.title: Module 6 Lesson 3 Mastery Checkpoint
checklist: I understand the compilation check performed by the @Override annotation
I know that @Override catches spelling typos and parameter mismatches immediately
I know that @Override has RetentionPolicy.SOURCE and zero runtime cost
I understand why equals(Object) vs equals(MyType) is a classic bug without @Override
I know that @Override can be used on interface method implementations
I know that applying @Override to static, private, or final methods causes compile errors
I understand how @Override protects code during superclass refactorings
I always annotate every overridden method with @Override as an industry best practice
I can explain accidental overloading vs intentional overriding in interview problems
I can fix compiler errors triggered by broken @Override annotations
